title: Testing for Reviewer Anchoring in Peer Review: A Randomized Controlled Trial
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether reviewers in academic peer review anchor to their original scores when given new information during a rebuttal process. The authors focus on a specific question: after a reviewer first scores a paper, then sees corrected evidence, do their revised scores remain biased toward their initial judgments compared with scores from reviewers who saw the corrected version from the start? Although the study is about peer review rather than classroom learning, it is relevant as an analogue evidence base for how people update judgments after receiving additional digital information.

To test this, the researchers ran a randomized controlled trial with 108 participants who were PhD students or PhDs with recent computer-science publications, recruited from nine U.S. research universities. Participants reviewed the same mock conference paper in a simulated peer-review setting over Zoom. The experimental group first saw a flawed version of the paper, then was shown the corrected animated figure after being told the original display had been frozen by technical error; they could then revise their scores and comments. The control group saw only the corrected version from the start. The paper used an animated GIF versus a frozen frame as the manipulation, and participants were asked to score multiple dimensions of paper quality plus an overall score.

The main finding was that the manipulation successfully changed participants’ initial judgments, especially on the Evaluation category, but the revised scores in the experimental group did not differ significantly from the control group. In other words, the study found no significant evidence of anchoring in this peer-review setting. The authors conclude that while rebuttals may often have limited impact, their experiment did not show that anchoring explains the lack of score changes. They note limitations including the modest sample size, the artificiality of the simulated review context, and the possibility that the task did not fully reproduce real conference-review dynamics.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial, but it studies reviewer anchoring in academic peer review rather than any K-12 educational technology or science learning intervention. Because it is not an intervention study relevant to the target education outcome domain, it does not provide usable evidence for the requested taxonomy.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact on K-12 science learning outcomes or educational practice; it reports a null finding on anchoring in conference peer review. No learner outcome, teacher outcome, or institutional K-12 effect is estimated.
